opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the central problems in AI control. The basic setup is: you've got some AI system doing a huge amount of work, maybe millions of actions a day, and you have a very limited budget of trusted human labor. Humans are expensive and slow, so maybe you can carefully look at something like a tenth of a percent of what the AI does. The question is how to spend that budget so it catches an AI that is actually trying to do something bad.

The naive approach is random spot-checking. If the AI only needs to do one bad thing to win, say inserting a backdoor or exfiltrating its own weights, random auditing of 0.1% of actions gives you roughly a 0.1% chance of catching that particular action. That's terrible. But the situation isn't quite that bad, because a scheming model probably can't succeed with one fully innocuous-looking action. It has to do something that's at least somewhat unusual, and that gives you a handle.

So the approach we've focused on is using a cheaper monitor to triage. You have a trusted model, typically weaker but one you're confident isn't colluding, read everything the untrusted model does and assign a suspiciousness score. Then you send the most suspicious actions to humans. Now your 0.1% isn't random; it's the top 0.1% by suspiciousness. If the attack has to look even modestly weird, that's a big improvement.

A few things make this more interesting than it first sounds.

First, auditing isn't only about catching the attack before it causes damage. It's also about incriminating the model. If you catch an AI red-handed trying to sabotage you, that changes your situation a lot. You can study the attempt, train monitors on it, use it as evidence to convince people the risk is real, and maybe stop deploying the model. So even one catch is enormously valuable, which means the AI faces asymmetric stakes: it might need to stay hidden across many attempts, while you only need to win once.

Second, you can do more than just audit or not audit. There's a spectrum of interventions. For moderately suspicious actions you can resample: ask the model to redo the step and see whether it does something different. You can defer to a trusted model and take its less capable output. You can edit the action to remove the sketchy part. These are much cheaper than human review, so you reserve humans for the very top tail and use automated responses for the wide middle band.

Third, you should think about where the budget goes over time. Early in a deployment you might want to audit more heavily, since that's when you learn whether the model is behaving and calibrate your monitors. And actions differ in how dangerous they are. A command touching security-critical infrastructure deserves more scrutiny than one editing a README, so risk-weighting the budget matters.

And then there's the question of whether human review is even reliable. If the AI is smart, a human reading a diff might just miss the subtle bug. So part of the work is making audits more effective: giving reviewers tools, letting them run the code, asking another model instance to explain what the action does, and checking whether that explanation holds up.

The overall picture is that limited audit capacity isn't hopeless, but it pushes you into thinking carefully about the game you're playing against the model: how strategic it can be, how often it needs to attack, how distinguishable the attacks are, and how to allocate a scarce resource across all of that. A lot of our research is basically building concrete testbeds where a red team plays the scheming AI and the blue team designs protocols, and we measure how much safety you can buy with a given amount of human oversight.

r001.rationale: It contrasts random spot-checking with sending humans the actions a monitor scores as most suspicious, and says this should improve the chance of catching attacks.

r002.rationale: It says random auditing of 0.1% of actions gives roughly a 0.1% chance of catching a particular attack action, making that action unlikely to be audited under random selection.

r003.rationale: It mentions that the AI may need to stay hidden across many attempts, but does not say safety depends on forcing repeated attack attempts that almost always fail.

r004.rationale: It describes the value of catching an attack, but does not compare the cost of defeating an attack with and without detecting it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that auditing is basically the mechanism by which you convert a small amount of scarce, trusted labor into a lot of safety. The core setup in AI control is: you've got this untrusted model doing a huge volume of work, and you've got some much smaller budget of trusted oversight, and the question is how you allocate that budget so that if the model does try to do something bad, you catch it before it matters.

The key constraint is exactly what you said: human review capacity is tiny relative to the volume of actions. If the model is writing a hundred thousand pull requests, you can't have humans read all of them. So you need a cheaper, automated layer in front — typically a trusted monitor, which is a weaker model you're confident isn't colluding with the policy — that scores every action for suspiciousness, and then you send only the top few percent to humans. The humans are the expensive, high-precision resource, and the monitor is the cheap, lower-precision filter that decides what they look at.

And then the thing that makes this actually work against an adversary, rather than just against random mistakes, is that the auditing has to be coupled to a credible consequence. If a human looks at an action and determines that the model was genuinely trying to, say, insert a backdoor or exfiltrate its weights, that shouldn't just be "okay, we blocked that one action." That should be a huge deal — you shut everything down, you investigate, you treat it as evidence the model is misaligned, you probably stop deploying it in that configuration. Because the model, if it's scheming, is reasoning about its odds. It knows that every time it attempts something, there's some probability it lands in the audited slice. If getting caught once is catastrophic for it, then it has to be very confident it won't be caught, and a modest audit rate with a decent monitor can push its success probability way down.

There's an asymmetry that helps you here, which is that the attacker usually needs to succeed at a small number of things, and you only need to catch them once. So even if you're only auditing two percent of actions, if the monitor is doing a reasonable job of concentrating the suspicious stuff into that two percent, the model's expected number of attempts before getting caught can be quite low. That's very different from the situation where you need to catch every single bad action — that you basically can't do with limited review.

I'd also say the human in the loop matters less for volume and more for being the trust anchor. The monitor can be fooled. The model might find ways to make malicious actions look innocuous to a weaker model. But a competent human reviewer who's been told "this is flagged, look hard at it" is a much harder target, at least for the kinds of actions we're worried about in the near term. So the auditing budget is really about buying yourself that hard-to-fool backstop in the places where it's most valuable.

The honest caveat is that this gets harder as the models get more capable relative to your monitors and your humans. If the model is doing things humans can't evaluate even when they stare at them, auditing doesn't save you in the same way, and you need other approaches. But for the regime we're likely to be in for the next few years — models that are very useful but not wildly superhuman — I think budgeted auditing is one of the highest-leverage safety techniques we have, and a lot of what we do at Redwood is trying to figure out how to squeeze the most out of that budget.

r001.rationale: It says a trusted monitor scores every action and sends the most suspicious actions to humans, describing this targeted selection as more useful than random auditing.

r002.rationale: It says only a small fraction of actions are audited and that the model must be confident an attack will not land in that audited slice.

r003.rationale: It discusses repeated attempts before being caught and says the expected number can be low; it does not say safety depends on forcing repeated attacks that almost always fail.

r004.rationale: It describes consequences for detected attacks but does not compare the cost of defeating an attack with and without detection.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between catching a particular attack and deterring attacks in the first place. If you can only afford to audit a small fraction of what the AI does, you probably can’t rely on a human happening to review the one action that would cause a catastrophe.

But suppose the AI needs to make a bunch of attempts before it succeeds, and each attempt carries some chance of being caught. Then even a relatively small audit budget can be useful. You might catch an early attempt and shut down the system before it gets to a successful one. That depends quite a lot on what you do when you catch it: noticing something suspicious and then continuing as before doesn’t buy you much.

You also don’t have to allocate human review uniformly. You can use a cheaper monitoring system to flag suspicious actions, and spend your human review budget on those. The hard question is whether an AI trying to attack you can reliably find actions that are dangerous but don’t look suspicious to your monitor.

So I’d want to evaluate the whole setup adversarially: give an attacker the opportunity to work around the monitor, enforce the actual human review budget, and see how often it succeeds before being caught. The useful quantity isn’t just how accurate the auditor is. It’s the probability that the attack succeeds before your process gives you a reason to stop.

r001.rationale: The response recommends using a cheaper monitor to flag suspicious actions for human review, but does not compare raising a classifier threshold with selecting actions randomly.

r002.rationale: It says a small audit fraction cannot be relied on to review the particular action that would cause a catastrophe, communicating that any specific attack is unlikely to be audited.

r003.rationale: It describes an attacker making multiple attempts before succeeding, but does not say those attempts almost always fail or that forcing repeated failures is a necessary source of much of the safety.

r004.rationale: It discusses catching and stopping attacks, but does not compare the cost of defeating an attack with and without detecting it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t necessarily need to audit every action. You need to make it sufficiently hard for the AI to predict which actions will get audited, and sufficiently likely that an attempted attack gets caught.

Suppose you can afford to review only a small fraction of what the AI does. You could use a cheaper monitor to flag suspicious actions, and spend most of your human review budget on those, while also auditing some actions at random. Then the question is: can the AI reliably find an opportunity to cause a catastrophe that both gets past the monitor and is unlikely to receive human review?

One important distinction is whether catching an attack lets you stop the whole process. If you catch the AI trying something malicious and can shut it down before it gets many more opportunities, auditing can be quite powerful. If it can keep trying indefinitely, even a pretty good chance of catching each attempt might not be enough. So I’d think about auditing as part of a larger system: limiting opportunities to attack, detecting attempts, and having a response that actually prevents subsequent attempts.

r001.rationale: The response proposes focusing human review on monitor-flagged actions while also auditing randomly, but it does not judge raising a classifier threshold to be probably better than random auditing.

r002.rationale: It raises as a question whether an attack could be unlikely to receive human review; it does not state that any particular AI attack is unlikely to be audited.

r003.rationale: The response discusses the risk of indefinite attempts, but does not identify repeated attempts that almost always fail as a necessary source of much of safety.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison between the cost of defeating an attack without detection and the cost of defeating one while detecting it.
